summary: The day is judgement, not code: seven steps lend themselves to multiple-choice questions on when to ship a rule, why replies vary, what to fix first in a prompt, what a new chat knows, when to fine-tune, how to check a method and what may be pasted, and only the constraints step has behaviour a Python check can see (an answer line tested against the allowed words); none of it lends itself to calling a model, which the runtime cannot do.

steps.title: AI, machine learning and deep learning
steps.reason: The nested definitions are quiz material, and the triage function on the page only illustrates a hand-written rule, so a Python task would test nothing the step teaches. The step does teach a judgement with named wrong ways (Google's first rule: six tickets is not data, a hand-written rule is not machine learning, a learned rule copies bad labels), which fits a choice task.

steps.title: Generative AI and how a large language model writes
steps.reason: Tokens and sampling have no behaviour a check can see without a model, and simulating the weighted dice roll needs randomness the checks cannot pin. Why one prompt gives two replies is a judgement the page names three wrong readings of (temperature 0 is fully deterministic, the model looks facts up, the model has seen the desk's tables), so it fits a choice task.

steps.title: Prompt engineering and zero-shot prompting
steps.reason: Prompts are typed text sent to a model the runtime cannot reach, so no Python task fits. Round 1 gives a judgement the page names the wrong ways of: what to add first when a zero-shot prompt invents tiers (context before examples, and a fluent reply that fails every success criterion is still a failure).

steps.title: Few-shot prompting and constraints
steps.reason: The step's own code checks each answer line against the allowed words, and the mistakes it names give a different return value: a substring test passes "This is probably high.", leaving out unsure rejects the escape hatch, and round 1's invented tiers must be caught. A short function on lists of strings stays inside the runtime and the page.

steps.title: Instructions, guidelines, iteration and dialog state
steps.reason: The page shows dialog state as a table of what each turn sends, never as code, so a Python model of a message list would rest on a structure the page does not teach. What a new chat knows and when to start fresh against sending a follow-up is a judgement the page names the wrong ways of, which fits a choice task.

steps.title: Fine-tuning and conditioning
steps.reason: Training is week 6 and nothing here runs, so no Python task fits. The "when a team reaches for each" table is a judgement the reader can get wrong in the ways the page names (examples in a prompt change the model, fine-tune first so it remembers), which fits a choice task.

steps.title: Hallucinations and how to check an answer
steps.reason: The worked case is pandas, which the runtime does not load, so the AttributeError cannot be reproduced in a check. What a developer does with a confident count_by reply is a judgement with named wrong ways (trust the plausible name, rely on a prompting technique alone, check docs for a version the desk does not pin), which fits a choice task.

steps.title: Responsible use and security
steps.reason: The page says names and connection strings are removed by hand and read before pasting, so a Python redactor task would teach against the step. Its sorting table (paste after redaction, never, paste) is a judgement whose wrong ways the page names: trusting desk.redact, pasting the employer's code, pasting a credential line.

tasks.title: Rule or model
tasks.idea: The desk has six labelled tickets and wants priorities set automatically. Which plan matches the page? Right: ship the hand-written rule now; it counts as AI but not machine learning, and the team moves to a model trained on labelled tickets once the conditions grow too complex to maintain.
checks: Train a model on the six tickets because a learned rule beats a written one catches skipping Google's first rule: machine learning needs data, and six tickets is not data.
Call the if rule machine learning because it predicts a priority catches the marketing reading the page warns about: nothing was trained, so it is AI in the broad sense only.
Train on last year's tickets because a learned rule cannot repeat a past mistake catches the trade-off the page's table names: a learned rule copies whatever the old labels got wrong.
tasks.q: The desk has its six labelled seed tickets and the hand-written triage(title) rule, and the team wants every new ticket's priority set automatically. Which plan matches the page?
options: Train a model on the six tickets: learned rules beat written ones.
Ship the if rule, calling it machine learning since it predicts.
Ship the written rule; train a model once it grows unmaintainable.
Train on last year's tickets: learned rules never repeat old mistakes.
tasks.explain: Google's first rule says not to be afraid to launch without machine learning, because machine learning requires data, and six tickets is not data. The if rule is AI in the broad sense but not machine learning, and a team trains a model once the heuristic grows unmaintainable.

tasks.title: Two replies to one prompt
tasks.idea: A teammate sends the same triage prompt twice and gets high, then normal, for the same title. Which explanation holds? Right: each token is sampled from a probability distribution, so replies vary, and even at temperature 0 the docs say results are not fully deterministic.
checks: The model looked the ticket up in the desk's database and the row changed catches the belief that the model looks facts up or has seen the desk's tables; it sees only its context window.
Setting temperature to 0 makes every reply identical, so the first run had a bug catches reading temperature 0 as a guarantee; the docs say a small amount of variation is still possible.
The first reply was right and the second is broken, so the first is the answer to keep catches treating a printed reply as a promise; each reply is one sample, and a fluent one can still be false.
tasks.q: A teammate sends the same triage prompt twice and gets high the first time and normal the second for the same title, Checkout button frozen. Which explanation holds?
options: Each token is sampled, so replies vary even at temperature 0.
The model looked the ticket up again, and its row changed.
Temperature 0 gives identical replies, so one run had a bug.
The first reply is right and the second broken; keep the first.
tasks.explain: A model writes by picking each next token from a probability distribution, and nothing in that loop looks a fact up, since the model sees only its context window. The docs say that even with temperature set to 0 the results will not be fully deterministic, so each reply is one sample, never a promise.

tasks.title: Fixing a zero-shot prompt
tasks.idea: "Write a triage rule for our support tickets." comes back with P1 to P4 tiers and made-up response times. What do you add first? Right: context: the three priorities, their SLA hours of 4, 24 and 72, and the output wanted, one priority and one reason line per ticket.
checks: Add a few labelled example tickets and nothing else catches reaching for examples before context; the page says the first fix to a zero-shot prompt is usually context, before examples.
Keep the reply because it is well written and covers every case catches judging a reply by how it reads; round 1 reads well and fails all three success criteria.
Send the same one-line prompt again until the tiers come back right catches hoping sampling fixes a prompt; the model saw one sentence and answered for a generic help desk, and it will again.
tasks.q: The prompt Write a triage rule for our support tickets. came back with tiers P1 to P4 and made-up response times. What is your next move?
options: Add three labelled example tickets, one per priority, first.
Keep the reply: it reads well and covers every case.
Resend the same prompt until the tiers come back right.
Add context first: the desk's priorities, SLA hours and output.
tasks.explain: The model saw one sentence, so it answered for a generic help desk, and the first fix to a zero-shot prompt is usually context, before examples. Examples alone would still leave it guessing the SLA hours and the shape of the answer.

tasks.title: Constraints
tasks.idea: The reader writes broken_answers(lines), which takes the answer line of each triage reply as a list of strings and returns, in the same order, the lines that are not exactly one of high, normal, low or unsure. For example, broken_answers(["This is probably high.", "normal", "unsure"]) returns ["This is probably high."].
checks: A sentence that contains an allowed word, such as "This is probably high.", is reported; a substring test like "high" in line lets it through.
"unsure" is not reported; an allowed list of only the three priorities forgets the escape hatch the constraint adds.
A tier the desk does not have, such as "P1" from round 1, is reported along with the others, in the order the lines came.
tasks.q: Round 3's constraint allows exactly one of high, normal, low or unsure on each answer line. Write broken_answers(lines), which takes the answer lines of a reply as a list of strings and returns a list of the lines that are not exactly one of those four words, one entry per broken line, in the order the lines came. For example, broken_answers(["This is probably high.", "normal", "unsure"]) returns ["This is probably high."].
tasks.tests:
assert broken_answers(["This is probably high.", "normal"]) == ["This is probably high."], "a sentence that only contains an allowed word is reported"
assert broken_answers(["unsure", "low", "high", "normal"]) == [], "unsure and the three priorities are not reported"
assert broken_answers(["P2", "high", "P1", "P2"]) == ["P2", "P1", "P2"], "every broken line is reported, in the order the lines came"

tasks.title: Dialog state
tasks.idea: Yesterday's long chat ended with a good round-4 reply. Today you open a new chat and type "Triage these three tickets the same way as before." What happens, and what do you send instead? Right: the new chat starts empty and knows nothing about yesterday, so you paste the complete round-4 prompt with today's titles.
checks: The assistant remembers yesterday's priorities, so the short message is enough catches the belief that a chat assistant remembers; every turn re-sends the conversation, and a new chat holds only its own messages.

Go back to yesterday's chat and keep adding follow-ups there instead catches ignoring drift; old turns can roll out of the window and long contexts lose accuracy, so a fresh chat with a complete prompt often beats a long patched one.

Send a follow-up turn naming the broken rule, as with round 3 catches using a follow-up where nothing is in the window to fix; a follow-up works only because the previous reply is in the context window.
tasks.q: Yesterday's long chat ended with round 4's good reply. Today you open a new chat and type Triage these three tickets the same way as before. followed by three new titles. What happens, and what do you send instead?
options: It remembers yesterday, so the short message is enough.
The chat starts empty, so send the complete round-4 prompt.
Return to yesterday's chat, whose first instructions stay for good.
Follow up with Use the rules from round 4. as after round 3.
tasks.explain: Every turn re-sends the whole conversation and a new chat holds only its own messages, so the priorities and rules have to be in its prompt again. A follow-up works only because the earlier reply is in the window, and a long chat drifts as old turns roll out of it.

tasks.title: Prompt or fine-tune
tasks.idea: A teammate wants the model to use the desk's three priorities on every request and proposes fine-tuning. The desk has three labels, six titles and one team decision. What does the page advise? Right: prompt first, since all of it fits in the window and is minutes to try; fine-tune only when the examples outgrow the window and the team accepts a training job and its evaluation.
checks: The three examples in the prompt already changed the model, so it will know the priorities in a new chat catches blurring conditioning with fine-tuning; examples steer through the window and the model's parameters never change.

Fine-tune first, because a prompt lasts only one conversation and so is never the right tool catches skipping the order OpenAI's guide gives: prompting may be all you need, and fine-tuning is slow to try.

Few-shot prompting is a small fine-tune, so the two cost the same to try catches the confusion the page opens with; fine-tuning is a second training pass with a training file, conditioning is text in a prompt.
tasks.q: A teammate wants the model to use the desk's three priorities on every request and proposes fine-tuning it. The triage needs three labels, six titles and one team decision. What does the page advise?
options: Rely on the prompt's examples: they already changed the model's parameters.
Fine-tune first: a prompt lasts one conversation, a fine-tune every request.
Prompt first: all of it fits the window and takes minutes to try.
Pick freely: few-shot prompting is a small fine-tune, equally cheap.
tasks.explain: OpenAI's guide says prompt engineering may be all you need, and fine-tuning earns its place when there are more examples than fit in one request's context window and the team accepts a training job and its evaluation. Examples in a prompt condition the model for that conversation only, and its parameters never change.

tasks.title: Checking a suggested method
tasks.idea: A reply says DataFrame.count_by("priority") groups and counts in one call. The desk pins pandas 3.0.6. What do you do before it goes in? Right: find the entry in the pandas 3.0 reference and run the line; the reference lists no count_by, the run raises AttributeError, and the fix is df["priority"].value_counts().
checks: Use it, since pandas has count and grouping and the name fits them catches overreliance on a plausible, confidently stated name; a hallucination reads exactly like a correct answer.

Ask again with "say I don't know if unsure" and use the method if it comes back the same catches treating a prompting technique as proof; the docs say these techniques reduce hallucinations but do not eliminate them.
Check the reference for the newest pandas release, where any new method would appear catches skipping the version; the check goes to the docs for the version the desk pins.
tasks.q: A reply says DataFrame.count_by("priority") groups and counts in one call, and the desk pins pandas 3.0.6. What do you do before the line goes in?
options: Use it: pandas has count and grouping, so it fits.
Ask again with Say I don't know if unsure and trust a repeat.
Check the newest pandas reference, where new methods appear first.
Check the pandas 3.0 reference and run the line first.
tasks.explain: A hallucination is stated confidently and reads like the real thing, so a claim about a library is checked in the docs for the version the desk pins and then run: the 3.0 reference lists no count_by, the run raises AttributeError, and df["priority"].value_counts() is the fix. Prompting techniques reduce hallucinations but do not eliminate them.

tasks.title: What goes into a public chat
tasks.idea: A stack trace from the desk holds mysql://desk_app:s3cret@db.internal:3306/ticket_desk and a customer's name and email, and you want help from a public chat assistant. What do you paste? Right: the trace after removing the host, user, password, name and email by hand and reading it again.
checks: The trace after running it through desk.redact catches trusting the helper's name; it hides emails only, leaves the name and the user, and its pattern happens to match s3cret@db.internal so the line only looks clean.
The trace as it is, since the assistant needs the exact error catches pasting credentials and personal information, which never go into a public chat.
The redacted trace together with transform.clean_events so the assistant sees the code catches pasting the employer's code, which goes only to an assistant the employer has approved.
tasks.q: A stack trace from the desk holds mysql://desk_app:s3cret@db.internal:3306/ticket_desk and a customer's name and email, and you want help from a public chat assistant. What do you paste?
options: The trace after desk.redact, which cleans the connection string and email.
The trace after removing host, user, password, name and email by hand.
The trace as it is: the assistant needs the exact error.
The redacted trace, plus transform.clean_events so it sees the code.
tasks.explain: Credentials and personal information never go into a public chat, and desk.redact hides email addresses only: it leaves the name and the user, and the line looks clean only because its pattern happens to match s3cret@db.internal. Names and connection strings are removed by hand, and the result is read before it is pasted.
